newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN WHEAT BOARD SLAMS DOOR ON MARKETER.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN WHEAT BOARD SLAMS DOOR ON MARKETER.

text.p: South Africa's Wheat Board has slammed the door on an agricultural marketing company which is trying to market wheat less than a year before the board is due to be phased out, industry officials said on Tuesday.

The Wheat Board is the last of South Africa's agricultural marketing boards to practise single-channel marketing and is due to adopt a free market system by October 31 next year when the current winter grain marketing scheme runs out.
The board on Monday obtained a Supreme Court order against agricultural marketing company Propermark, barring it from selling or trading wheat.
"Within a year or so we will be deregulated and Propermark jumped the gun and advertised saying they also were buying wheat," said a Wheat Board spokesman, who asked not to be named.
"They have put themselves in our position, buying and selling wheat -- while there is only one (present marketing) channel," he told Reuters on Tuesday.
The spokesman said under South Africa's new Agricultural Marketing Act which has not yet taken effect, the board would have about a year left before switching to a free market system.
He said producers have voted to retain the present marketing system at the beginning of the new marketing year in November 1997.
Agriculture ministry spokesman Helmuth Schlenter said the new act could come into force by the end of this year.
"The law should be promulgated within the space of one month, by the end of this year," Schlenter said.

The legislation passed in parliament last month outlaws statutory agricultural market controls and accepts that market supply and demand is the best method to ensure the efficient allocation of resources.
It also means the demise of mostly-white commodity control boards -- like the Wheat Board -- which controlled the marketing of agricultural products for almost seven decades.
Industry observers said the Wheat Board's action went against the government's intention to deregulate the marketing of agricultural products.
Propermark officials were not available for comment on Tuesday.

But the company's managing director, Nico Botha, told Business Day newspaper on Monday the board had issued permits for direct trade between farmers and buyers under a new permit system to other traders.
"We are very disappointed with the judgment, but will take it on appeal on Thursday. Why did the board refuse our permit and grant permits to other big companies?," Botha told the newspaper.
The Wheat Board spokesman said the industry was unsure what to expect from deregulation.
"You will not have a national marketing agency. There are 6,000 producers and only six buyers. There is a certain balance at the moment because we are the only marketer.
"At the end of the day, when you have a lot of small marketers and still only six buyers -- I don't know what the market will do".
